title: One bag at a time

hosts.Leyla: lives in Baku and loves a good plan
hosts.Sam: grew up in Manchester and once travelled with no plan at all

before.predict: How many plastic bags or bottles did you use this week? Guess: who in this episode started a big green project at home — Leyla or Sam?

chapters.title: Sam's plastic week
chapters.prompt: CHAPTER 1 SCENE: a kitchen table covered with a week of plastic rubbish — bottles, bags, coffee cups, food boxes — piled up high, a surprised man looking at it with his hands on his head, morning light

chapters.title: The bigger picture
chapters.prompt: CHAPTER 2 SCENE: a wide landscape split in two — on the left a green forest full of birds and animals, on the right cut trees and a factory with smoke, wind turbines and solar panels on a hill in the distance

chapters.title: What we can do
chapters.prompt: CHAPTER 3 SCENE: a sunny balcony in Baku with recycling bins in three colours, a cloth shopping bag full of vegetables, a reusable water bottle and a small plant growing in a pot, the Caspian sea in the distance

lines.t: Hi everyone, and welcome to the SpeakLab Podcast. I'm Leyla.
And I'm Sam. Today we're talking about the environment — and I did an experiment.
Oh, I love experiments. What was it?
For one week I kept every piece of plastic I used. Every bottle, every bag, every coffee cup. [sigh] By Sunday my kitchen table was full.
Full? In one week?
Yes. And most of it was single-use. I used it for five minutes and then threw it away.
That's the problem, isn't it? Plastic lives for hundreds of years. Pollution in the sea is terrible now.
So I decided to turn over a new leaf. Now I carry a cloth bag and my own bottle.
Good for you! But some people say: 'One person can't change anything. It's just a drop in the ocean.'
I hear that a lot. And it's true that the big changes must come from countries and companies.
Like renewable energy — sun and wind instead of oil and gas.
Exactly. And stopping deforestation. When we cut down forests, we lose biodiversity — thousands of animals and plants.
And the forests take carbon from the air. So every tree matters.
But I still think small actions count. If a million people do one small thing, it's not small any more.
I agree. My family started to recycle last year. Paper, glass and plastic in different bins.
Was that difficult?
At first, yes. [chuckle] My dad put everything in the wrong bin for a month. Now he checks everyone else's!
[laugh] The new environmental police. Do you think about your carbon footprint too?
A little. I take the metro more and I fly less. For me, sustainability means asking: do I really need this?
That's a great question. Buy less, buy better, use it longer. That's how we go green without stress.
Here's your question for your next SpeakLab call: what is one thing you could do this week for the planet?
Mine is no more coffee cups. See you next time!
Bye for now!
